text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's Austrian newspapers:
DER STANDARD
- Austria's ambassador to Peru Arthur Schuschnigg is among the hostages taken by the Peruvian guerilla group at the residence of the Japanese ambassador in Lima.

- Andreas Khol, chief whip of the conservative junior coalition partner, wants a special session of parliament to change privatisation laws in order to prevent Bank Austria from taking over Creditanstalt.

- The consortium around EA-Generali plans to take legal action against Bank Austria at the European Court of Justice because it says Vienna city government helps the bank. Should Bank Austria take over Creditanstalt potential savings could be worth 3.5 billion schillings.
- Creditanstalt workers' council prefers the consortium around EA-Generali.
- More than ten offers have been made for Austria's salt producer Salinen AG, which is to be privatised soon.
- The future partner of postal savings bank PSK should bring know-how. PSK plans to enter the private loan market.
- Sugarmaker Agrana expects profits to jump to 164.9 million schillings in the first half from 94.2 million schillings the previous year.
DIE PRESSE
- 38 percent of Austrians believe the introduction of a single European currency will worsen the country's economy.

- The possible takeover of Creditanstalt by Bank Austria is also having an influence on the Vienna city council. While conservatives, liberals and the far-right Freedom Party want to see Bank Austria completly privatised, the Social Democrats and Greens want the city to keep a minority stake of 25 percent.
- Should Austria's coalition fall apart because of the privatisation of Creditanstalt, prices on the Vienna stock exchange would fall.
- Investments worth 10.5 billion schillings and payments to the federal government are going to prove difficult for Austria's postal service this year and the next but in 1999 it could make a profit.
- The number of insolvencies this year rose to a new record high of 5,500. In 1997 a slow improvement is expected.
KURIER
- Bank Austria chief Gerhard Randa says Bank Austria and Creditanstalt are too small to survive on their own in the European Union.
- Austrian parliament expected to approve restructuring of postal monopoly on Friday, paving the way for partial privatisation.
WIRTSCHAFTSBLATT

- Austria's 1996 current account deficit in the 1996 balance of visible and invisible items is expected to reach 50 billion schillings, compared with 47.3 last year. An improvement is not seen by Austria's central bank for the next year.
